newsitem.title: USA: Hill & Knowlton decision may help insurers.
newsitem.headline: Hill & Knowlton decision may help insurers.

text.p: A Florida judge's decision on Tuesday to dismiss damage claims against public relations firm Hill & Knowlton, a WPP Group Plc affiliate, in the state's $1 billion Medicaid suit against the tobacco industry may be good news for insurers.

"This is not just good news for Hill & Knowlton, but probably for any insurers they might have," said Gregory Hopp, insurance industry attorney with the Chicago law firm Blatt, Hammesfahr & Eaton. Insurers have argued that policies sold to tobacco companies after the mid-1960s specifically excluded payment for tobacco-related losses.
But policies sold to other third parties that worked with the tobacco industry, such as Hill & Knowlton, did not contain such tobacco exclusions.
Therefore, some policyholder attorneys argued that the third parties involved in tobacco litigation would have a stronger case for coverage under their liability policies.

"Hill & Knowlton was probably the number one candidate for third party liability to come in and surprise" the insurance industry, said Alan Levin, managing director at Standard & Poor's. "That was the one area where we thought there might be some potential," he said.
But, if the courts dismissed the damage claims against the third parties, as Florida did with Hill & Knowlton, they might have little need to turn to their insurers.

In his decision, state judge Harold Cohen said Hill & Knowlton's actions took place too far in the past for it to be considered a partner in the conspiracy to misinform the public alleged by Florida in the suit.
The judge pointed out that Florida's racketeering statute was not passed until 1977, nine years after Hill & Knowlton ceased providing any public relations support to the tobacco industry.

Hopp said the judge's decision may show that "the liabilities here, to the extent there are any, are going to be confined to the cigarette manufacturers, rather than these concentric circles of retailers, distributors and professional service providers."
Insurers may still face some expenses related to the defense of those third parties, said Robert Carter, a policyholder attorney with the Washington, D.C.-law firm McKenna & Cuneo.
And, it was not clear what impact Florida's decision might have on other third parties in other states.
But, if Florida, a state where the courts have looked favorably on plaintiffs' actions, dismissed these claims, that might bode well for third parties in other states, Hopp said.

"If even the Florida courts don't look at those claims, don't think much of those claims, that probably is good news not only for Hill & Knowlton, but at least to finally put to bed the idea that their insurers are going to get hit," he said.
Levin said he believes the judge's decision "means that the insurance industry is even more remote from this problem.
"The insurance industry should be rejoicing," he said.
